title: Youngsan University Holds Memorial, Fundraiser for Nepal Flood Victims - Seoul Economic Daily
description: Youngsan University Holds Memorial, Fundraiser for Nepal Flood Victims  Seoul Economic Daily
publisher.title: Seoul Economic Daily
full_article:
Youngsan University's International Student Support Center holds a fundraising event at its Haeundae campus on the 21st to honor victims of the floods in Nepal and aid residents of the affected areas. Photo courtesy of Youngsan University

BUSAN — Youngsan University has extended condolences and relief support to the people of Nepal and to Nepali students on its campus following recent large-scale flooding.

The university's International Student Support Center held a memorial ceremony and a donation drive at the Haeundae campus on the 21st to honor those killed in the Nepal floods and to help rebuild the affected areas, the university said on the 22nd.

Faculty members and students observed a moment of silence, praying for the repose of the victims and a swift recovery in the stricken region.

The ceremony was organized to console Nepali students grieving the disaster and to convey that the university community stands together across nationalities.

Alongside the memorial, the university collected donations through a designated account to provide practical relief to affected residents.

"Nepal is a valued neighbor to members of our university and the homeland of their families," said Ban Hyun-jung, head of the International Student Support Center. "We hope the donations gathered with sincerity, along with our remembrance of the victims, will bring some comfort and strength to bereaved families and residents of the affected areas."

The university said it will continue to promote the values of respect and consideration among its members beyond nationality and culture, and to fulfill its social responsibility by standing with global neighbors facing disasters.

title: Nepal’s Foreign Minister Holds Flurry of UNGA Sideline Talks on First Day in New York - nepyork.com
description: Nepal’s Foreign Minister Holds Flurry of UNGA Sideline Talks on First Day in New York  nepyork.com

full_article:
NEW YORK — Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal held a series of bilateral meetings Monday with senior officials from the European Union, Poland, Bhutan, Portugal and Japan on his first day in New York for the high-level week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Khanal arrived at John F. Kennedy International Airport at 8:50 a.m. Monday on Qatar Airways Flight 703. He was welcomed by Lok Bahadur Thapa, Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations; Dadhiram Bhandari, Nepal’s consul general in New York; and officials from Nepal’s permanent mission to the United Nations.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is welcomed by Lok Bahadur Thapa, Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations, and Dadhiram Bhandari, Nepal’s consul general in New York, after arriving Monday at John F. Kennedy International Airport to attend the high-level week of the 81st U.N. General Assembly. Photo from Shishir Khanal’s Facebook page.

After arriving in New York, Khanal said in a social media post that he was leading Nepal’s delegation during the General Assembly’s high-level week. He thanked Thapa, Bhandari and mission officials for the welcome and said he would begin a series of bilateral meetings that afternoon to advance Nepal’s priorities on the international stage.

Thapa also welcomed Khanal to New York and wished him a productive stay and successful meetings during the General Assembly.

Talks Span Europe, South Asia and Japan

Khanal began the afternoon with a meeting with Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive transition, at U.N. headquarters.

Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive transition, welcomes Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal for talks at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

Khanal expressed gratitude for the European Union’s sympathy and solidarity following Nepal’s recent Bhotekoshi floods, according to Nepal’s permanent mission to the United Nations. The two sides discussed the Nepal-E.U. partnership and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation on recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, and Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meet at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

Khanal then met Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski at U.N. headquarters. The discussions focused on expanding Nepal-Poland relations, cooperation in areas of mutual interest and coordination at the United Nations and other multilateral forums.

According to Poland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the meeting covered Poland’s support for what it described as positive political and economic changes in Nepal, including through expert assistance. The Polish ministry also said the two sides discussed Nepal’s support for Ukraine and what it described as Russia’s exploitation of Nepali citizens who are being forced to fight in Ukraine.

The Polish Foreign Ministry’s account of the meeting was posted on social media Monday. Poland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The Polish ministry later deleted that post and published a revised statement that omitted the reference to Russia’s exploitation of Nepali citizens. In its revised post, the ministry said: “The talks focused on Poland’s support for positive political and economic developments in Nepal, including expert assistance, and appreciation for Nepal’s support for Ukraine.”

In the afternoon, Khanal met Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay at Bhutan’s permanent mission in New York. Tobgay reaffirmed Bhutan’s solidarity with Nepal following the recent floods and conveyed best wishes for the recovery and reconstruction of affected communities.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal speaks with Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay during a meeting. Lok Bahadur Thapa, Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations, and Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai also joined them. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

Khanal later met Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel at U.N. headquarters. The two officials discussed bilateral relations and areas of mutual interest.

Portugal’s Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel, right, meets with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

In the evening, Khanal met Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi at U.N. headquarters. Nepal and Japan marked the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations this year, with both countries having highlighted cooperation in areas including trade, investment, energy, infrastructure, tourism, education and culture.

Japan’s Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal hold talks at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

The meetings generally focused on bilateral relations and issues of mutual interest. Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai, Thapa and other Nepalese officials also took part in the meetings.

Climate and Reconstruction on Nepal’s Agenda

Khanal is accompanied by Rai, Joint Secretary Krishna Prasad Dhakal and other officials.

Nepal is scheduled to host a side event on Sept. 25 titled “Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future.” The event will focus on climate change and its effects, particularly in the Himalayan region.

The Bhotekoshi floods are expected to feature prominently in Nepal’s discussions during the General Assembly. The disaster, which struck Aug. 26, caused extensive damage in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other areas along the river system. Nepal’s Foreign Ministry has described the event as an unprecedented disaster and said recovery and reconstruction will require international support.

Nepal is expected to highlight climate justice, the impact of climate-related disasters, the concerns of least-developed and landlocked developing countries, and international cooperation on investment, trade, recovery and reconstruction.

Prime Minister to Join General Assembly

Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to leave for New York on Sept. 22 and address the General Debate on Sept. 24. He is also scheduled to meet with U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres.

According to Nepal’s Foreign Ministry, Shah is scheduled to return to Kathmandu on Sept. 26, while Khanal is expected to remain in New York through Sept. 29.

The Foreign Ministry said the Nepali delegation to the high-level week includes Khanal, Rai and other senior government officials.

title: Recurring tech failures rattle Nepal’s stock market - The Kathmandu Post
description: Recurring tech failures rattle Nepal’s stock market  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Repeated technical glitches at Nepal’s Stock Exchange have raised concerns over the reliability of the country’s capital market, with experts warning that such disruptions are undermining investor confidence and putting more than Rs4.5 trillion in investors’ assets at risk.

On February 17, 2026, the Nepse index was shown to have plunged by 885.32 points, or 33.34 percent, after the closing prices of some companies were displayed as zero. The stock exchange attributed the unusual fall to a technical error.

On July 23, about 15 minutes after trading had closed, the Nepse website and trading management system (TMS) simultaneously showed the index falling by 1,008 points, or around 37 percent, to 1,717 points. The sharp decline was not an actual market movement but the result of a data or technical error.

On September 21, Nepse halted share trading for the day after a technical problem at Data Hub Pvt Ltd, the data centre used by 72 brokers.

These are only some recent examples. At different times, disruptions have been blamed on technical problems at Nepse, broker firms, YCo Pvt.Ltd (the company managing the trading system), and data centres.

Experts say such recurring disruptions are among the reasons Nepal’s capital market has failed to make significant progress even after more than three and a half decades.

With problems piling up at the country’s sole stock exchange, investors are also being hit by periodic disruptions at broker firms, data centres and the company managing the trading system, says share market expert Niraj Giri.

He says such problems keep recurring because Nepal’s stock market has lacked long-term thinking and planning from the beginning.

“The problems keep recurring because Nepse and other stakeholders have not been sensitive enough to the development and expansion of the capital market,” he said. “Even when I was working at the Securities Board [of Nepal], I had been calling for the introduction of a good, internationally standard trading system, but the market continues to face problems time and again.”

Giri said although the trading system, data centre and other infrastructure are managed by different entities, Nepse should exercise overall control and bear ultimate responsibility for ensuring the market’s reliability.

Such incidents, he said, erode investor confidence in the stock market and create risks to the security of their assets.

Investors have also complained that a limited number of companies have a monopoly over key systems used to conduct share trading, leading to repeated problems.

Investor Subhash Chandra Dhungana said such a monopoly was one reason the problems remain unresolved. “Investors are already struggling to maintain confidence in the market,” he said. “Repeated problems only add to their uncertainty.”

While technical problems in trading systems can occur, Dhungana said the lack of alternative arrangements was a serious weakness.

“The market was closed on Monday, but even now no one knows whether it will open tomorrow,” he said. “Why is there such uncertainty? How can investors feel reassured in such a market?”

Of the 90 broker firms currently operating, 72 were using Data Hub’s data centre. A ransomware attack was detected at the data centre at around 4 am on Sunday and this affected the systems of the 72 broker forms. Nepse suspended trading on Monday following a written request from the Stock Brokers Association.

Brokers, however, said the problem was not of their making.

Narendra Raj Sijapati, former president of the Stock Brokers Association, said brokers had been restricted from managing key infrastructure such as data centres and trading systems, which remained under the control of a small number of business groups. “Whenever there is a technical problem, responsibility is shifted from one place to another. But investors and brokers are always the ones who suffer,” he said.

The Nepse board met on Monday evening to discuss the incident and agreed that trading would not be suspended on Tuesday even if the Data Hub problem remained unresolved, according to a source. “If the problem at Data Hub is resolved, the entire market will open. If not, trading will be allowed through the remaining 18 brokers,” the source said.

The data of the 18 other brokers are hosted by other companies. Those brokers had also requested that trading be allowed on Monday, but Nepse did not agree.

Nepse spokesperson Murahari Parajuli said the market had been closed following a request from the affected brokers after the technical problem emerged at Data Hub. He said there was a possibility of regular trading resuming on Tuesday.

The Securities Board of Nepal (Sebon), Finance Ministry and Prime Minister’s Office were also informed about the market closure and sent their respective teams to gather information.

Sebon chairman Gopal Bhatta said the board was investigating the incident.

“As the regulator, I have sent a team and asked it to investigate,” he said. “The board has instructed Nepse to conduct a thorough study into the circumstances that led to the suspension of trading and submit a report by September 28, along with recommendations to prevent such incidents from recurring.”

The board said it had taken serious note of the technical problem at the data centre where the servers of 72 of the 92 licensed securities brokerage companies were hosted. It deployed a five-member inspection team led by a deputy executive director to identify the technical problems and determine why trading had to be suspended.

The incident, which was detected at Data Hub’s data centre on Sunday morning, remained unresolved until around 11 am on Monday. Data Hub subsequently asked the affected brokers, through YCo, the company managing their trading systems, to suspend trading.

YCo later informed the Stock Brokers Association that the incident had affected multiple systems and services, including the trading management system, systems related to Central Depository System and Clearing , payment gateways and other interconnected services. The affected systems were isolated as a precaution.

According to YCo, the network connection between the data centre and Nepse meant the disruption could pose cybersecurity, operational and data-security risks. It said continuing trading while the impact and extent of the incident were still being assessed could create additional risks.

title: Opinion | What the Bhotekoshi flood revealed about Nepal’s health system - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | What the Bhotekoshi flood revealed about Nepal’s health system  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Disasters are often measured in lives lost, property damaged and infrastructure destroyed. However, something deeper must accompany the assessment: the strength and resilience of the institutions responsible for response. How effectively can these systems keep functioning when normal conditions collapse? Nepal’s recent Bhotekoshi flood became a real-time examination of the disaster health preparedness, leadership, coordination and resilience of the state and, by association, its institutions.

The response of our health system in particular was encouraging. It responded far more effectively than it might have a decade ago. The Health Emergency Operations Centre (HEOC) was activated, hospitals continued accepting referrals, disease surveillance was expanded, Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) were mobilised, and mental health services were able to reach the affected communities. Regular situation reports helped maintain operational awareness and supported decision-making during a rapidly evolving emergency.

This progress reflects a key aspect of institutional learning since the 2015 earthquakes and subsequent emergencies. Investments in preparedness, emergency coordination and health-sector capacity were visible throughout the post-earthquake policy response. But preparedness should not be confused with resilience. The flood ultimately revealed that the Nepali health system does not lack institutions or expertise, but the challenge lay in effectively integrating many capable actors into a unified operational system.

The response brought together the Ministry of Health and Food Safety, HEOC, provincial and district health authorities, hospitals, the Nepali Army Medical Corps, Armed Police Force (APF) and Nepal Police Medical Services, EMTs, United Nations agencies and humanitarian organisations. Each contributed valuable resources and expertise. Did these actors operate as one coordinated system or as multiple systems responding simultaneously?

Coordination and command are not the same thing. Coordination enables organisations to communicate and share information. Command ensures that resources are directed where they are most needed. The flood highlighted a challenge familiar to emergency-management systems worldwide: many organisations may perform well individually, yet overall effectiveness can still suffer if operational leadership is fragmented. Future disasters are likely to become more complex, making it increasingly important to strengthen operational command while preserving collaborative coordination.

Emergency Medical Teams provide a useful example. Over the past decade, Nepal has invested significantly in EMT development. Provincial governments, hospitals, security agencies and humanitarian organisations have all developed deployable medical capabilities. During the response to the flood, these teams proved invaluable. However, as the number of deployable teams grows, governance becomes increasingly important. Future emergencies will require a mechanism capable of registering, verifying, deploying and monitoring EMTs under a common framework. A National EMT Coordination Cell could provide that function.

The flood also highlighted the oft-overlooked challenge of mass fatality management. Many victims were swept long distances downstream, while others were recovered only after prolonged exposure to water, making visual identification difficult or impossible. The recovery of decomposed, bloated and, in some cases, fragmented human remains required a coordinated effort involving security agencies, forensic experts, health authorities and local administrations. The systematic collection of biological samples, documentation of remains, DNA profiling and scientific identification of victims represented a significant advancement in Nepal’s disaster-response capability and demonstrated the growing role of forensic medicine in humanitarian emergencies.

The tragedy also exposed important infrastructural limitations. Existing mortuary facilities and refrigerated storage capacity were insufficient to accommodate the unusually large number of recovered bodies over an extended period. In many locations, the absence of adequate mortuaries and body chiller facilities created operational and public health challenges, necessitating timely burial of unidentified bodies after appropriate forensic documentation and sample collection had been completed.

As climate-related disasters increase in frequency and severity, Nepal should further strengthen its mass fatality management capacity through specialised training, expanded mortuary and body-storage infrastructure, enhanced forensic preparedness, DNA identification systems and standardised protocols that can be rapidly activated during major emergencies

Disaster response is fundamentally a logistics exercise. Throughout the response, supplies were mobilised through government agencies, health facilities, security forces and humanitarian partners. While commodities generally reached affected populations, logistics remains one of the least visible yet most critical components of emergency management. Greater attention to inventory visibility, stock management, warehousing and supply-chain intelligence could significantly strengthen future responses.

Another lesson from the flood was the critical importance of health information management and operational situational awareness. During rapidly evolving emergencies, decision-makers require accurate, timely and interoperable information to assess health needs, track disease risks, monitor the availability of medical resources and prioritise interventions. Although regular situation reports were produced, future responses would benefit from stronger integration of data streams from hospitals, EMTs, laboratories, local authorities and humanitarian partners into a unified information platform. Strengthening digital health emergency information systems, standardising reporting formats and improving real-time data sharing across all levels of government would significantly enhance decision-making, resource allocation and overall response effectiveness during major disasters.

The role of security agencies deserves special recognition. The Nepali Army Medical Corps and APF Medical Services contributed far beyond traditional rescue functions. Immediate deployment of Emergency Medical Response Teams (EMRTs), Medical evacuation, mobile treatment services, field-level health support and surge response capacity all became essential elements of the health response. Future planning should focus on stronger civilian-military integration, common reporting standards and shared operational frameworks.

While the emergency phase has largely been contained, the most demanding work still lies ahead. The recovery phase should restore health, wellbeing and resilience of the affected populace. In the months ahead, priorities should include rebuilding damaged health facilities, restoring essential services, strengthening disease surveillance, supporting mental health recovery and ensuring continuity of care for vulnerable populations. Recovery should also be viewed as an opportunity to address pre-existing system weaknesses rather than simply restoring conditions to their pre-disaster state.

Recovery planning must extend beyond reconstruction. Long-term challenges such as displacement, disrupted livelihoods, psychosocial distress, chronic disease management and the needs of women, children, older persons and marginalised communities will require continued attention. Investments in preparedness, community resilience and risk reduction should therefore become central elements of the rehabilitation agenda. Moving forward, Nepal must create a stronger, more coordinated, more resilient and more disaster-ready health system for generations to come.

In Nepal, the Nepal Stock Exchange (Nepse) suspended stock trading on September 21 due to a technical problem at the Data Hub Pvt Ltd data center, whose services were used by 72 brokers. Kathmandu Post reports that the incident was detected on Sunday morning, and as of around 11:00 on Monday, the problem had not yet been resolved.

According to the publication, a ransomware attack was detected at the data center at around 4:00, affecting the systems of 72 brokerage companies. Trading was halted following a written request from the Stock Brokers Association.

Risks to market operations

YCo Pvt Ltd, which manages brokers' trading systems, said the incident affected the trade management system, services related to the central depository system and clearing, payment gateways, and other associated services. The affected systems were isolated as a precautionary measure.

YCo said that because of the data center's network connection to Nepse, continuing trading before assessing the scale of the incident could have created risks for cybersecurity, operations, and data protection. Nepse representative Murahari Parajuli said the exchange was closed at the request of affected brokers and that regular trading could resume on Tuesday.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

According to an anonymous source for the publication, the Nepse board agreed on Monday evening not to suspend trading the following day even if the problem at Data Hub was not resolved. In that case, transactions were to be allowed through 18 brokers whose data are hosted by other companies. These brokers had also asked for trading to open on Monday, but the exchange did not agree.

A series of technical failures

This is not the first technical incident on Nepal's stock market. On February 17, 2026, the Nepse index mistakenly showed a decline of 885.32 points, or 33.34%, after the closing prices of shares in some companies were displayed as zero. The exchange explained this as a technical error. On July 23, about 15 minutes after trading ended, the Nepse website and the trade management system simultaneously showed the index falling by 1,008 points, about 37%, to 1,717 points. There was no actual market movement at that time.

Experts and investors interviewed by the publication believe that recurring problems in the operation of the exchange, brokers, data centers, and trading systems undermine confidence in the market and jeopardize investors' assets worth more than 4.5 trillion Nepalese rupees. The Securities Board of Nepal sent an inspection team and instructed Nepse to submit by September 28 a report on the reasons for the trading halt and recommendations to prevent similar incidents.

title: Opinion | Rain is coming again. This time, Nepal must be prepared - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Rain is coming again. This time, Nepal must be prepared  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal has not yet finished burying its dead from the Bhotekoshi disaster. The rescue teams are still out, the missing lists still open, and now a low-pressure system building over the Bay of Bengal is projected to bring heavy rain across the country from September 24 to 28. Meteorologists largely agree that enormous rain is coming. Where it will be heaviest, and on which of those five days, remains unsettled. Given how often heavy rain in this season has cost Nepal lives and property, that uncertainty is not a reason to relax.

Several forecast models point towards more than 400 millimetres of rain, with one outlier model suggesting a figure as high as 741 mm. To put it in context, the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) itself classifies anything above 200mm in 24 hours as extremely heavy. The scale of rainfall forecast is closer to half of the monsoon’s worth compressed into five days. Some experts even forecast that central Nepal—where the flood in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system left a trail of destruction last month—is one of the regions with heightened possibility of heavy rain. The risk, therefore, has already increased.

Heavy rain does not automatically become a disaster. Whether it does depends substantially on how well information reaches people beforehand and how seriously they act on it. That is why the three tiers of government, along with the media and relevant organisations, need to put this forecast in front of the public now—plainly, with the actual numbers, not dressed up to frighten and not played down to reassure.

Nepal has already faced this test twice in the past two years, and the results were far from encouraging. Heavy rainfall in 2024 overwhelmed rescue capacity even inside Kathmandu Valley. Surrounding districts took heavy damage from flooding and landslides in the same spell. The BP Highway, battered in that period, still has not been fully restored, and stretches of road elsewhere in the country are in no better shape.

None of the three tiers of government has yet shown it can mount an effective response once a flood or a landslide is already underway. Even modest interventions have struggled to hold. Preparedness efforts must be expedited in the days before the rain arrives, rather than counting on a response capacity that has already been tested and found short.

Much of this risk is also structural and will outlast this particular storm. Roads and settlements across Nepal sit close to riverbanks, without any real practice of distinguishing land fit for habitation from land that isn’t, or building accordingly. Fixing settlement patterns, construction standards and information systems is a longer project than five days allow. For now, government at every level needs a concrete plan for this specific window.

Information needs to reach the public before Thursday, not after. Arrangements for rescue, temporary shelter and relief distribution need to be in place in advance, even if they end up unused. A gap in response to a disaster the state saw coming days out is utter negligence.

Individual preparation matters too. Every household should weigh how exposed its home and workplace actually are. Where a residence sits near a riverbank, an unstable slope or low-lying ground, extra vigilance is warranted now. A safe route to higher ground should be worked out in advance, not improvised mid-flight. Deciding in advance what to carry, who carries what, and where to go will matter enormously.

title: Balendra Shah’s UN appearance draws diplomatic interest in New York - The Kathmandu Post
description: Balendra Shah’s UN appearance draws diplomatic interest in New York  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s scheduled address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly has generated considerable interest among diplomats in New York, where he is due to arrive on Tuesday to lead the Nepali delegation.

Two of Shah’s aides, Pradip Pariyar and Subash Sharma, reached New York on Sunday to oversee preparations, logistics and the prime minister’s engagements. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal arrived in New York on Monday evening, local time, along with Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai and other foreign ministry officials.

“The diplomatic community in New York is curious,” a Nepali diplomat based in the city told the Post over the phone. “There is curiosity about his presence and what he will say, given his age and his rise to power following last year’s Gen Z movement.”

Leaders are generally allotted 15 minutes to deliver their statements during the General Debate, although speakers can go beyond the allotted time.

Shah is scheduled to address the General Assembly on September 24, with his speech expected to focus on climate action, climate justice and compensation for climate-related losses, particularly in the wake of the devastating Bhotekoshi floods of August 26.

He is also expected to highlight the vulnerability of low-carbon-emitting countries to the effects of climate change and draw global attention to the concerns of mountain nations.

“The speech of the prime minister is ready,” an aide to Shah told the Post. “It focuses on the recent Bhotekoshi floods, climate justice and the vulnerabilities of mountain countries, among other issues.”

Shah has received more than 500 emails and suggestions through various channels on issues he should raise with the international community.

“Our prime minister is the youngest leader speaking at the General Assembly this time. Second, the UN and its various agencies have a number of agendas concerning youth. So naturally, the New York-based diplomatic community is interested in what he says,” said the diplomat, who asked not to be named.

“He has attracted global attention following the Gen Z movement,” the diplomat said. The election of Shah as the world’s youngest serving prime minister and the mandate secured by the Rastriya Swatantra Party in the March elections have also heightened interest in his visit, the diplomat added.

“There are not only curiosity but also expectations from the prime minister,” the diplomat said. “Since he is young and comes with a strong mandate, there are expectations about what he will offer.”

The August 26 floods in the Bhotekoshi river and their impact downstream were widely reported by international media, further raising interest in Nepal’s message on climate change at the UN, according to the diplomat.

“Countries like ours that are facing the perils of climate change want to listen to our prime minister and hear what he has to offer,” the diplomat said.

Besides the diplomatic community, Nepalis living in different parts of the United States are also expected to gather in New York on September 24 to express solidarity with Nepal’s call for climate justice as Shah addresses the General Assembly.

With around 75 percent of the population of the Global South being young, other leaders are also interested in what the young Nepali prime minister will present at the General Assembly, the diplomat said.

Besides seeking climate justice for low-carbon-emitting countries, Shah is expected to speak about the political changes in Kathmandu following the Gen Z movement and the March elections. He will also highlight Nepal’s contribution to global peace through UN peacekeeping operations and touch on contemporary global, regional and domestic issues.

Despite the interest surrounding his visit, Shah is not scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with visiting heads of government or state on the margins of the General Assembly, according to officials.

“We have received several requests from heads of government and others for meetings with the prime minister. But, besides the meeting with the UN secretary-general António Guterres, he is not meeting with anyone else due to time constraints,” the diplomat said.

description: In Nepal, 95% of Law Commission drafts did not become laws — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS

full_article:
In Nepal, the Law Commission, established to draft and review legislation, remains sidelined from key lawmaking processes. Since the 2015 Constitution came into force, it has drafted and submitted 43 bills to the government, but about 95% of them have never become laws, Kathmandu Post reports.

The government's legislative programme for 2026–2027 includes 166 bills: 97 new ones and 69 amendments to existing laws. Only two of them are directly linked to the Law Commission's recommendations — bills concerning the commission itself and artificial intelligence.

Over the past fiscal year, the body drafted five bills. They concerned the National Youth Council, compensation for victims of wrongful investigations and prosecutions, the Nepal Scouts organisation, the rights and development of Dalit communities, and amendments to the law regulating the commission's work.

Drafts have not advanced for years

Among the documents that received no further progress is a 2019 bill on the establishment, registration and operation of public organisations. It was intended to simplify the creation of such organisations by citizens and establish clearer legal foundations for non-governmental organisations. According to the publication, disagreements between the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Women, Children and Senior Citizens halted the document's progress.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Another draft, submitted in April 2020, concerned updating legislation on the acquisition of land for public purposes. It provided for standards on compensation, resettlement and rehabilitation. The document did not advance because of disputes between the Ministry of Land Management, the Ministry of Home Affairs and the National Planning Commission. A draft aimed at accelerating the construction of infrastructure facilities of national priority was also not implemented.

Dispute over the commission's leadership

Nepal's Law Commission has had no chairperson or vice-chairperson since its last head, Jaggeshwar Subedi, left office on 30 July 2025. At the same time, the government proposed amending the 2007 Nepal Law Commission Act so that its chairmanship would pass to the law minister.

Law Minister Sobita Gautam stated that the reform should turn the commission into a professional centre for drafting bills within the state apparatus. Under the proposed model, the commission would prepare the initial text of a document, the relevant ministry would be responsible for policy, and the bill would go to parliament after approval by the Cabinet of Ministers.

Former commission chair Madhav Poudel opposed this approach, stressing the need for independent expert leadership. The commission's secretary, Indira Dahal, also reported staff shortages and budget cuts. The commission is currently working, among other things, on a draft law on egg donation, studying the pay and benefits of public officials, and preparing recommendations on repealing, reviewing or amending outdated provisions.

Cooperation with Bhutan and Japan

At a meeting with Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay, the sides discussed bilateral relations and strengthening cooperation on climate change. During talks with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, the Japanese side expressed condolences to the victims of the natural disaster. According to Japan’s Foreign Ministry, Tokyo intends to support Nepal from the emergency phase through medium- and long-term recovery. Talks with Poland and the European Commission

At a meeting with Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, the diplomats discussed the development of relations and the expansion of bilateral cooperation, as well as more effective interaction at multilateral platforms, including the UN. A Polish statement said that Sikorski condemned the exploitation of Nepalese citizens in the Russian army.

Khanal also met with European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera. They discussed the Nepal-EU partnership, as well as cooperation on the recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction of areas affected by flooding in Bhotekoshi.

title: After Hormuz, Nepal and wildfires, people demand action to make polluters pay - Climate Home News
description: After Hormuz, Nepal and wildfires, people demand action to make polluters pay  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
Anne Jellema is executive director of 350.org; Mads Christensen is executive director of Greenpeace International; and Amitabh Behar is executive director of Oxfam International .

On Monday, global petitions with a collective total of more than 2 million signatures were presented to the United Nations, calling on governments to introduce binding mechanisms to make fossil-fuel companies and the super-rich contribute to the costs of the damage they have created.

The petition signatures were received by Selwin Hart, the UN Assistant Secretary-General for Climate Action, in New York during the UN General Assembly, sending a clear message to governments: there is no more room for excuses.

If governments are serious about resilience, energy security and protecting people from an increasingly unstable world, they must make the companies profiting from the fossil-fuel economy pay their fair share. Because the crisis we are facing is no longer some distant threat. It is unfolding in real time, and it is exposing the extraordinary costs of an economy still built around fossil fuels.

For more than six months, the Strait of Hormuz, the channel through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed without a second thought, has been closed, contested or effectively unusable. Tankers sit at anchor. Insurance premiums have gone through the roof. Petrol pumps from Los Angeles to Lagos have felt the tremor. It has taken a war to remind the world just how much of our daily lives still rests on a single, fragile artery of fossil fuels.

At the other end of the same emergency, a glacier came down on the Nepal–China border in the last week of August. A wall of ice, rock and water tore through the Bhote Koshi and Langtang valleys. It has been described as one of the deadliest disasters in the region's modern history, unfolding in a landscape where the world's glaciers are retreating and destabilising at a pace scientists have been warning about for years.

And this came only weeks after hundreds of thousands of people were displaced — not by ice, but by fire. Europe has experienced its worst wildfire season in more than a decade. Homes have been lost across Spain, Portugal, France, Greece and the UK. Firefighters and civilians have been killed battling the blazes, while damage and reconstruction costs continue to reach extraordinary levels.

These are not separate crises. They are different expressions of a world becoming more volatile, while the fossil-fuel economy continues to generate enormous profits for those at the top and pushes the costs onto everyone else.

Communities absorbing cost

Because the crisis we are facing is no longer some distant threat. It is unfolding in real time, and it is exposing the extraordinary costs of an economy still built around fossil fuels. One thread runs through all of these events: a global economy still organised around the profits of a fossil fuel industry that has known, for decades, exactly what it was doing to the planet.

At a moment when governments are gathering in New York for the UN General Assembly to talk about security, resilience and economic competitiveness, it is worth spelling out what "security" - or the lack of it, driven by our economy’s dependence on oil - actually means this year for ordinary people around the world: 35,000 excess deaths in Europe due to heat; the highest food prices in three and a half years; $700 billion in economic losses, threatening countless jobs and livelihoods, from a war and a closed oil chokepoint whose consequences are nowhere near over.

Meanwhile the companies that extracted, refined, shipped and sold the fuel behind all of this continue to report extraordinary profits. Households are paying more for energy. Governments are spending billions on disaster response, on reconstruction, on emergency deployments of firefighters and aid. Communities are absorbing the cost of a system they didn't design and don't control. We pay. They profit.

This is not a coincidence, and it is not inevitable. It is a political choice, repeated year after year, to let the companies most responsible for the climate crisis hoard the wealth they generate while the rest of us carry the risk.

Taxes and fines needed

That is why, together with communities and campaigners in dozens of countries have spent the last three years building the case for a simple, overdue idea: polluters should pay for the damage they have caused. Not through voluntary pledges or distant net-zero promises, but through binding mechanisms, climate damages taxes, surtaxes on fossil fuel profits, and fines ring-fenced for recovery and adaptation that put real money where the harm actually is. This is how we take the profit out of destruction and protect the generations to come.

The response has told us we are not alone in thinking this. Our petitions calling on governments to make polluters pay have now gathered a collective total of over 2 million signatures from people across every region of the world.

The case for making polluters pay has moved into the mainstream

That is not a fringe demand. It is what happens when people watch a choke-point war spike their fuel bill, watch a glacier take a thousand lives, watch their own summer holidays rearranged by fire. They draw the obvious conclusion: the people who caused this should be paying for it – not profiting from it.

We hear the objection already forming: that this is not the moment, with wars underway and economies fragmenting, to burden industry further. We would say the opposite is true. If governments can mobilise trillions for war, for bailouts and for new fossil fuel infrastructure, they can mobilise the political will to tax the companies that caused this crisis.

Money for clean energy and resilience

That money can go straight to the people paying for it, through cheaper, cleaner, more secure energy, and through funding for communities on the frontline of floods, fires and glacial collapse. There isn't an excuse left. There is only a choice about where power and money go next. Every dollar we don’t spend now on adaptation, resilience and cutting emissions, we burn many times over later: on disasters we could have prevented and economies we scramble to fix too late.

This year's UNGA should be the moment that choice gets made in public. Governments arriving in New York will talk about resilience, about energy security, about protecting their citizens from an unstable world. Let them explain on the record why a fossil fuel industry that has spent decades profiting from that instability should not be the one paying to fix it so wrecking the planet no longer pays off.

The fires, floods and storms won't just go away. The system that keeps producing these disasters, and keeps paying the same companies for the privilege, will not change itself unless political leaders step up. It is on all of us to make sure they hear, as loudly as possible, that the time for excuses has run out.
